description: Red Bug Planet: four CSE students from Dhaka, new to hackathons, in love with Mars and turning bugs into features. Building an interactive web project with NASA data. Looking for a designer, data viz/analysis skills, and good storytellers. Beginners welcome!
summary:
Launch Command is a 3D browser game that puts players in the role of a mission designer and flight controller. Players choose one of three real NASA missions (Apollo to the Moon, Perseverance to Mars, or Juno to Jupiter) and design a spacecraft by selecting power systems, antennas, computers, and science instruments. Six live meters (mass, power, budget, data, communications, and time) show how every choice affects the mission.

Players then pick a real rocket, count down, tilt the vehicle, separate stages, reach orbital speed, and send the spacecraft on its way. Random events like solar flares test the design, and a final mission report grades the result.

The game turns real space engineering trade-offs into play, helping students understand why missions succeed or fail. Built in Dhaka for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, it makes space science accessible to anyone with a browser.
details:
What it does:

Launch Command teaches how real space missions are designed and flown. The player completes the full chain: choosing a mission, designing the spacecraft, selecting a rocket and launch site, flying the launch, and grading the mission result.

How it works: There are three missions based on real NASA missions: the Moon (Apollo), Mars (Perseverance, Jezero Crater), and Jupiter (Juno). Each has its own objective, budget, science target, and most critical constraint (time on the Moon, communications at Mars, power at Jupiter). The player builds a spacecraft from options for structure, power (solar or RTG), antenna, computer, attitude control, battery, and science instruments, while six meters track mass, power, budget, data, comms, and lifetime. The player then picks one of seven rockets (including Atlas V, Titan IV-B, Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, SLS, and Saturn V). A rocket that cannot lift the spacecraft is flagged, so mass and capacity matter. During flight, the player follows a countdown, tilts the rocket along the ascent path, drops the spent stage on Mission Control's call, and accelerates to 7.7 km/s to reach orbit before leaving orbit for the target. Random events such as micrometeoroids, solar flares, weak sunlight, and comms glitches affect results. A final report shows what worked and what did not.

Tools and technologies: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in a single file; Babylon.js 6.49 for 3D graphics; Web Audio API for generated sound effects; Web Speech API for the Mission Control voice; Google Fonts (Lilita One, Quicksand, Michroma).

Creativity: Instead of only flying a rocket, players must design the mission first, so they learn that engineering trade-offs decide success. Each destination has a different dominant challenge, and a Mission Control voice and on-screen guides teach beginners as they play.

Factors we considered: Playability on phones and desktops (touch and keyboard controls), simple explanations for beginners, scientific realism in mission names, rockets, and trip times, and no installation needed.

Impact: Students can learn how real missions are planned and why every kilogram, watt, and dollar matters, which can inspire interest in space and engineering careers.
